activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A child's age is said with a number word, like 'I am four.'
story:
Josephine stood at the sand table. She wanted to pour sand into the red cups. But Ben had all the cups. He looked grumpy and held them tight.

Miss Ana came over. "Ben, ask Josephine how old she is," she said. Ben looked at Josephine. "How old are you?" he asked. Josephine held up four fingers. "I am four," she said. Ben held up his fingers too. "I am four too!" he said. He smiled now. He gave her three cups. Josephine poured sand into each one.

Then the whole class sat on the rug. Miss Ana sang a counting song. "One, two, three, four, five," they all sang. Josephine sang too. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Her voice was loud and happy. She clapped at the end.

At play time, Ben pointed out the window. "Look, a nest," he said. Two birds sat in it. "How many birds?" Josephine asked. "One, two," said Ben. They counted together. Then Miss Ana called, "Snack time!" Josephine held Ben's hand and walked to the table with him. "I am four," she said again, just to hear it. "And you are four too."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: A book's title is its name.
story:
Milan went to the store with his dad. The store had a big book shelf. Milan wanted his favorite book. He could not see it. He only saw a blue cover way up high.

"Dad, can you fetch that blue book?" asked Milan. Dad reached up. The book was too tall. Then it began to slip. Dad caught it just in time. There was no big fall, no crash. The book was safe in Dad's hands.

Dad turned it over. He pointed to the front. "This says The Sleepy Bunny," he said. Milan looked at the words. He traced them with his finger. "That is its name," said Dad. Milan smiled. "The Sleepy Bunny is the book I want!" Dad opened the front cover. Together, they began to read.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: At school, children take turns on the playground slide.
story:
It was Ava's first day of school. She held her mama's hand. The room had blocks and paint and a pink table. Ava's tummy felt funny. "Who will play with me?" she asked. "I will stay a little while," said Mama.

At recess, Ava saw the slide. She ran to it. A boy named Sam was at the top. He slid down. Then he ran to go again. Ava stood in front of him. The teacher said, "Sam, we take turns on the slide." Sam walked to the back of the line. Ava got in line too. She waited. Then it was her turn. Whee! Down she went, fast.

After recess, the class ate bread and apples. Ava learned that waiting made the slide fun for everyone. Sam sat next to her. "Want to slide again?" he asked. "Yes!" said Ava. Mama waved from the door.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: On a tablet, you tap the screen with your finger to choose things.
story:
Beatrice was at Grandma's house. She wanted to draw a picture. Grandma had a soft gray case on the table.

Grandma showed her the tablet. Beatrice pressed her whole hand on the screen. She pressed hard. The screen did nothing. "Hmm," said Beatrice. "Why won't it go?"

"Try one finger," said Grandma. "Just a little tap." Beatrice lifted one finger. She gave the screen a gentle tap. The screen lit up! A tap made it come on.

"What is this?" Beatrice asked. She tapped a green square. The drawing app opened. There was a big white page. She tapped the blue color and drew a ball. Then she drew a broom, like the one Grandma used to sweep the floor.

"All done," said Beatrice. She tapped the top. The page closed. Grandma helped her slide the tablet back into its soft case.

"Bye bye, ball," said Beatrice, and patted the case.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Up and down are opposites.
story:
Lucy ran into the playroom. Her friend Ben was there too.

"I want the big teddy bear!" said Lucy. She reached up high on the shelf. It was too far.

Ben brought the small stool. Lucy stepped on it. Still too far. She reached and reached. Then the stool tipped. The toy cups fell down. Crash! One cup began to spill little blue beads all over the floor.

"Uh oh," said Ben.

Lucy sat down on the floor. She looked at the shelf, then at her hands. Then she had an idea.

"Up and down are opposites," said Lucy. "The teddy goes up. I pull him down!"

She pushed the shelf end of a long toy ramp. The ramp leaned up to the shelf. Lucy tapped the teddy's foot. He slid down, down, down, right into her lap.

"I got him!" Lucy hugged the teddy tight.

"Again!" said Ben. He tapped a small ball. It rolled down fast. Lucy tapped the big ball. It rolled down slow.

Mama came in with warm cocoa. "Careful, it's hot," she said. She set it on the table and cooled it with a puff of air. Lucy took one little sip. "Now it's cold enough!"

She smiled wide and gave the teddy a sip too.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: Grabbing a toy out of someone's hands can make them feel sad or angry.
story:
Adam ran to the sandbox. He saw a big red truck. His classmate Mia was holding it. Adam wanted the truck now.

Adam grabbed the truck out of Mia's hands. Mia's face got sad. Her eyes filled with tears. She began to cry. The playground felt noisy with her crying.

Adam looked at Mia's sad face. He gave the truck back. "Here, Mia," he said. "Your turn first." Mia stopped crying. She smiled. "You can have it next," she said.

Mia pushed the truck down the hill. Vroom! Then she rolled it back. "Now you, Adam," she said. Adam took the truck. "Thank you, Mia," he said. He pushed the truck fast. Mia clapped her hands. They took turns all morning. Then they sat together on the bench. "Best friends," said Mia. Adam smiled and rolled the truck to her feet.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
story:
Gabriel was building a big block tower at home. His cousin Mia came to play. "My turn?" asked Mia. Gabriel gave her one block. Then one more. They took turns, turn by turn.

Then Gabriel ran fast to get a red block. He bumped the tower with his elbow. Crash! All the blocks fell down. Mia's eyes got big. Her mouth turned down. "My tower," she said.

Gabriel felt something tight in his chest. What could help? He knew a word. "Sorry, Mia," he said. Then he picked up a block. Mia picked up a block too. They built the tower again, taller than before. "This one is ours," said Mia. She gave Gabriel a tight, happy hug until it made him laugh.

"Should we tickle the tower goodnight?" Gabriel whispered. Mia giggled. "Towers don't tickle," she said. "But you do!" And her fingers wiggled toward his tummy.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Flour is a dry powder that makes a little cloud when it is poured fast.
story:
Norah wants to make pancakes for her family. She pulls her stool to the big shiny counter. "I will cook!" she says. Daddy helps her get the bowl and the spoon.

First she cracks the eggs. Plop, plop. Then Daddy hands her the bag of flour. Norah tips it fast. Whoosh! A big white cloud puffs up. It lands on her nose. It lands on Daddy's nose too. "Achoo!" says Daddy. "You look like a snowman," says Mommy, laughing.

"Let's try again," says Daddy. He pours a new bag of flour slowly. This time there is no cloud. The flour just slides down, soft and quiet. "I can do it slow," says Norah. She takes her turn. Slow, slow, slow. No cloud at all. Mommy mixes the batter, and Daddy cooks the pancakes on the hot pan while Norah watches from her stool.

At breakfast, everyone has clean noses. "These are the best pancakes," says Mommy. Norah licks her fork. "I made them," she says. "Slowly, slowly, slowly."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A number word always means the same amount: 'three' always means three things.
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. She saw a big bowl of grapes. "Can I have three grapes?" she asked. Mom said, "Yes, you can have three grapes."

Iris picked one big grape. "Is this three?" she asked. Mom shook her head. "That is one," Mom said. Iris picked another grape. Now she had two. "Two," she said. She picked one more. "One, two, three!"

Her brother Leo wanted grapes too. "Can I have three?" he asked. Mom gave him three little grapes. Iris looked. His grapes were small. Hers were big. She counted his grapes. "One, two, three," she said. "Leo has three too!"

Then the clock on the wall began to ring. "Wash hands after grapes," said Mom. Iris put her grapes near Leo's plate so he could reach the bowl. Then she ran to wash her hands, singing, "One, two, three!"

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Dogs, cows and fish are all animals.
story:
Penelope went to the store with Mama. She wanted a new animal toy. "Let's look at the animal bin," said Mama.

Penelope found a little dog. "A dog!" she said. "A dog is an animal." She put it in the cart. Then she found a soft cow. "A cow!" she said. "A cow is an animal too." She put it in the cart too.

Then she saw a small orange fish. Penelope frowned. "This one has no legs," she said. "It cannot be an animal." Mama smiled. "Is a fish an animal?" Penelope asked. "Yes," said Mama. "Dogs, cows and fish are all animals." Penelope hugged the fish. "Hello, animal fish!" she said. The fish went in the cart.

On the way home, Penelope held her three toys. "One dog, one cow, one fish," she said. "Three animals!" She patted them gently. Then she whispered to the fish, "You can hop on my pillow tonight. No legs needed."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Crayons can melt if they are left in a hot car on a sunny day.
story:
Charles left his crayons in the car. The car sat in the sun all day. Now it was time for lunch, and then Charles wanted to draw.

After lunch, Dad got the crayons from the car. Charles peeked into the box. "They look funny," he said. He picked up the orange crayon. It bent like a worm. It was soft and squishy in his hand.

Charles tried to draw with it. The soft crayon made a fat, wet line. It looked different from before. Was it because of the hot car? The sun had made the car hot, and the crayons had gone soft and bendy.

"Can we draw with them anyway?" Charles asked.

"Let's try," said Dad. Charles pressed the orange crayon down. It made a big smudge, like a sunset. He made another one, and another. Soon the whole page was orange.

Charles held up his paper. "My crayons made a hot sun picture," he said. Dad put it on the fridge.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: The hairdresser puts a cape around your shoulders to keep cut hair off your clothes.
story:
Elias went to the mall with Mom. They walked past the toy store and the big fountain. Then they came to a hair salon. Elias was getting his very first haircut.

"Sit here," said the hairdresser. She put a big cape around his shoulders. It was blue and soft. Snip, snip went the scissors. Little hairs fell down. The hairs landed on the cape, not on his shirt. Elias giggled. "I look like a superhero," he said. The cape held all the hairs.

After the haircut, the hairdresser took the cape off. She shook it, and all the hairs fell away. Elias looked at his shirt. It was clean. He looked at the floor. The hairs were there. "The cape kept my shirt clean," said Elias. Mom smiled. "You look so big," she said. They walked out past the fountain. Elias waved at his car in the parking lot.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: You can pretend to take care of a doll or stuffed animal, like feeding it or tucking it into bed.
story:
Mohamed's teddy bear, Brown Bear, sat on the floor. He looked sad. His head was tipped over.

"Bear is sick," Mohamed said. "What can I do?"

His mother came close. "You can pretend to take care of him," she said.

Mohamed found a little cup. He held it to Bear's mouth. "Drink your medicine," he said. "Drink it all up."

Then he got a small blanket. He tucked Bear into bed. "Night night, Bear," he whispered.

Mohamed patted Bear's soft head. "Do you feel better now? Yes, you do."

He waited by the bed. His shadow fell over Bear like a hug.

Later, Mohamed found his toy bunny. Bunny looked sleepy. Mohamed smiled. "Don't worry, Bunny. I will take care of you too."

He got the blanket and wrapped Bunny up. "Time for medicine," he said, holding the little cup.

Mother watched from the door. "My Mohamed," she said softly, "you take such good care of your babies."

Mohamed kissed Bear and kissed Bunny. "Sleep tight," he said. "I will check on you after my snack."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Now means at this very moment.
story:
Arnaud loved the red robot at school. It had loud buttons and big wheels. He wanted to play with it today.

"Can I have the robot now?" Arnaud asked. "The robot is not now," said Miss Pia. "Ben has it now. You can have it after snack." Arnaud looked at his hands. Was now this minute? He clapped once. Yes, that clap was now, and then it was gone. Now meant right this minute, the very moment he was in.

Arnaud waited. He filled his cup with water at the little table. He ate his crackers. He drew a robot on paper. Was it after snack yet? Not yet. He watched Ben push the loud button again and again.

"Now you," said Miss Pia. Arnaud ran to the rug. He held the red robot. He pushed the button. The robot rolled fast, right now, this very minute. "Today I got the robot," Arnaud said. "Yesterday I did not. Tomorrow I will play with it again." The wheels spun and spun.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
Evan ran to the big paper on the grass. He wanted to paint the sky. He dipped his brush in the light blue paint. He made a big sky, soft and pale.

His friend Mia came over with a dark blue crayon. She drew dark blue under his sky. "That is not blue!" said Evan. "It is too dark!"

Mia held her crayon next to his sky. "It is blue too," she said. "Dark blue." Evan looked and looked. The paint was light. The crayon was dark. They put them in a row, lightest first, then darkest. "Both are blue," said Mia. Evan smiled and painted dark blue water under his light blue sky. "Thank you," he said. He gave Mia the polite little bow he did for guests. Then he painted one green leaf and one yellow sun, and Mia laughed and clapped.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: In English, there is a space between one word and the next.
story:
Colton wanted to write a note for Grandpa. It would say "GOOD NIGHT." Grandpa was tucking him in, and Colton wanted him to find the note by his bed.

Colton found his smooth blue crayon. He wrote all his letters in a big line. G-O-O-D-N-I-G-H-T. All the letters touched each other. There was no gap at all. They looked like one long, wiggly worm.

Grandpa came in. He picked up the note. He turned it sideways. He held it far away. Then he held it close. "Hmm," said Grandpa. "I cannot read this one."

Colton's tummy felt tight. He looked at Grandpa's storybook on the bed. Grandpa opened the front of the book first. The words sat in little groups on the page. Each group had a space after it. One word. Then a space. Then the next word.

Colton took his crayon again. He wrote GOOD. He lifted his crayon off the paper. Then he wrote NIGHT. The space sat between the two words. He held the note out. "Read it now," he said.

Grandpa smiled big. "GOOD NIGHT," he read. "I can read it now." He put the note on the pillow. He opened Colton's book to the front page. "We start here," he said.

Colton snuggled down. The note would stay by his bed all night. "Read it again tomorrow," he said. Grandpa turned the first page.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Christmas, many families decorate a tree.
story:
Sarah went to the big hall with Mama and Papa. There was a Christmas party. In the middle of the hall stood a tall tree. At Christmas, many families decorate a tree, Mama said. Sarah wanted to help.

She held a soft red ornament. She hung it on one branch. Then she hung a blue one there too. Then a gold one. Then a boat ornament, white with a little sail. All of them sat on one branch. The branch began to bend. The branch went down, down, down. Plop! The ornaments fell into the soft blanket below.

Sarah picked them up. She looked at the tree. So many branches, all empty. She hung one ornament on this branch. One on that branch. One, two, three, up and up. Papa brought her a stool, and she reached the high branches. The tree began to shine all over.

A little bell chimed somewhere. Sarah turned around. Grandpa was holding a tiny ornament with a bell inside. "Where should this one go?" he asked. Sarah pointed to the very top branch and smiled.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Adding white paint to a color makes it lighter, so red with white becomes pink.
story:
Kinsley sat at the little table in the playroom. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower on it. Kinsley looked in her paint box. She had red paint, blue paint, yellow paint and green paint. But there was no pink paint.

Kinsley made a red flower first. "Too dark," she said. Grandma's flowers were soft and light. Kinsley put her brush in the water jar. The water made a small sound. Swish, swish. She washed the red brush until it was clean.

Then Kinsley had an idea. She put red paint on her paper. She put white paint next to it. She stirred them together with her brush. Round and round she stirred. The red paint turned lighter and lighter. Now it was pink! Kinsley made a happy sound, a high little squeal.

She painted a big pink flower. Then she painted a green stem. She painted blue dots all around it. She painted a yellow sun up high. Mommy came in and looked. "What a pretty pink flower," said Mommy. "Grandma will love it." Kinsley held the card up to show her.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: An indoor cat uses a litter box as its toilet.
story:
Norah came home with a small cat. The cat was soft and gray. Norah held her teddy bear in one arm. The cat rode in a box.

Then Norah had a worry. "Where will the cat go potty?" she asked. Dad showed her a pan on the floor. "This is a litter box," he said. Norah touched the sand inside. It felt like tiny seeds. Dad let her pour a little more sand in.

The cat sniffed the box. She stepped in. She dug a small hole. Then she covered it up with her paws. Norah clapped her hands. "She used it all by herself!" she said. "What a smart cat." The cat jumped out and rubbed on Norah's leg. It felt warm and soft, like her teddy bear.

At bedtime, Dad tucked Norah in. The cat curled up at the foot of the bed. Norah patted her head. "Good night, cat," she whispered. The cat gave one tiny purr.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups.
story:
Weston ran to the playground with Dad. He wanted to go on the tall slide. But when he looked up, his tummy felt funny. His legs stopped walking.

"Are you scared?" asked Dad. Weston nodded. He felt sad, too. He wanted to slide like the big kids.

Then Dad sat down on the bench. "I was scared of slides once," said Dad. "I was a little boy then." Weston's eyes got wide. "You had scared feelings?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups." Weston thought about that. Grown-ups were so big. But they felt things too.

A girl came down the slide. She laughed and clapped. She looked so happy. Weston held Dad's hand. They climbed the stairs together. Weston sat at the top. His heart went boom, boom. He was excited now, not scared.

Down he went, fast, fast, fast. "Again!" he shouted. Then something surprised him. Dad went down the little slide too. Dad's hair flew up like wings. "Whee!" said Dad. Weston laughed and laughed.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: Cutting a square from one corner to the opposite corner makes two triangles.
story:
Juliette sat at the art table. She had a brown piece of paper. The paper was a square. It had four sides, all the same. Next to it sat a small circle of glue and a long rectangle of green paper.

Juliette wanted to make a sailboat. "I need two triangles for the sail," she said. She looked in the paper tray. There were no triangles. Only squares, circles and rectangles. She looked again. She waited. Still no triangles.

Her teacher, Miss Ana, came over. "Show me where you want the sail," she said. Juliette pointed to one corner of the brown square. Then she pointed to the corner far, far away from it. "Corner to corner," said Juliette. Miss Ana picked up the scissors. "Scissors are for grown-ups," she said. "I will cut on your line." Snip, snip. The square fell into two pieces. Juliette touched them. Two triangles! She clapped her hands.

Juliette glued the green rectangle down for the boat. Then she glued one triangle on top. Then the other triangle, right beside it. The sail stood tall. At snack time she took a small taste of her cracker, then ran back to look at her boat. "Sail away," she said, and pushed it gently across the table.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: A hairdresser uses a comb to keep hair neat while cutting it.
story:
Zoey sat in the waiting room with her mom. Today she would get her first real haircut. Her tummy felt a little sour and nervous.

A lady named Mia came out. "Ready, Zoey?" she asked. Zoey shook her head. "The scissors look big," she said.

Mia held up a little comb. "Watch what I do first," she said. She combed a small piece of hair. Then she made one little snip. Zoey leaned forward to see. Mia combed again. Then she snipped again.

"I can count," Zoey said. "One comb, one snip." Mia smiled. "You count with me," she said. Zoey sat up tall in the big chair. One comb, one snip. Two combs, one snip. The hair fell down like soft rain. Soon Zoey's hair was short and neat.

Mom clapped her hands. "You did it," she said. On the way home, they talked about dinner. Zoey looked in the mirror and turned her head. "I like my haircut," she said. "Can we come back and count again?"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Hanukkah, Jewish families light candles on a menorah for eight nights.
story:
Oliver went to the cultural center with Mama and Dad. Tonight there was a big party for Hanukkah. Oliver saw tables with candles. The candles were white and tall and very pretty.

"Can I touch one?" Oliver asked.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Fire is hot. Only grown-ups light them."

A lady named Ruth stood by a golden candle holder. "This is called a menorah," she said. "We light candles on it for eight nights."

Ruth lit a little helper candle with a match. She used it to light two candles. "We lit one candle last night," she said. "So tonight we light one more."

Oliver counted with his finger. "One, two," he said. "Last night was one. Tonight is two!"

"Right," said Ruth. She smiled at him.

Tomorrow there would be three candles. Oliver had a secret plan. He would count them all the way to eight. He would count slow, so the counting would last.

Mama bought him a warm latke from the food table. It smelled like potatoes and made his tummy feel happy. Oliver ate it while the candles glowed.

"Next year I count again," he said.

Ruth laughed. "Deal," she said.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Soon means in a little while.
story:
Violet put on her red boots at daycare. Today was painting day. But the paint cups were empty on the shelf.

"Can we paint now?" Violet asked.

Miss Ana smiled. "Soon," she said. "Soon means in a little while. First we eat snack."

Violet sat at the little table. She poured milk from her small cup. The milk was cold. She ate her banana, bite by bite.

"Now?" she asked again.

"Soon," said Miss Ana. "After we clean up."

Violet put her cup in the sink. She wiped the table with a sponge. The table went from wet to dry.

Then Miss Ana called the class to the art corner. "Paint is ready now," she said.

Violet dipped her brush in the blue paint. She made a big round circle. It looked like the moon.

"My moon is wet," said Violet. "It will be dry tomorrow. We can touch it tomorrow."

Yesterday her moon picture had been all wet too. Today it hung on the wall, dry and shiny. Tomorrow she would take it home.

After painting, Violet looked out the window. The snow was falling on the slide. Later, the class would go outside. Violet watched one snowflake land on the cold glass.

"Look," she said. "One snowflake. Now there are two."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Setting the cup down on the table before pouring keeps it still.
story:
Aubrey wanted to do it herself. Daddy made the toast and set it on her plate. Aubrey took the butter knife. She spread the butter. First one stroke, then another. The butter made a shiny path on the toast. "Look, Daddy, I did it!" she said.

Then came the milk. Aubrey held the cup in one hand. She poured with the other hand. The cup wiggled. Milk splashed onto the table. "Oh no," said Aubrey. Daddy wiped it up. "Try again," he said.

Aubrey looked at the cup. What if it sat down? She set the cup on the table. The cup stayed still. She poured the milk slowly. Not one drop spilled. The milk went up, up, up to the line. Aubrey picked up the cup and took a big drink. "The cup does not wiggle now!" she said. Daddy clapped his hands.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Toast is bread that has been heated until it turns brown and crunchy.
story:
Felix put two slices of soft white bread into the toaster. Miss Ana pushed the lever down. "We buy this bread from the bakery," she said. "Watch now."

The bread popped up. Felix touched one slice with one finger. It was warm. It was brown. It was crunchy. "The bread was white and soft," said Felix. "Now it is brown and crunchy!"

"That is toast," said Miss Ana. "Toast is bread that has been heated until it turns brown and crunchy." Felix sniffed the toast. It smelled warm and good.

Now Felix had a job. He took the little knife with the safe round edge. He dipped it into the butter. He spread the butter slowly, one, two, three strokes. The butter melted into the warm toast and went shiny.

Next came the milk. Felix held the cup with one hand. He poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. He licked a crumb off his thumb. His itchy sweater sleeve rubbed his chin.

He counted his work: one slice of toast, one cup of milk, zero spills. Miss Ana clapped her hands.

"Breakfast time," said Felix, and he took a big crunchy bite.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
story:
Evan wanted to paint a pumpkin at daycare. He looked in the paint cup. There was red paint. There was blue paint. There was yellow paint. There was green paint. But there was no orange paint. "I need orange for my pumpkin," said Evan.

His friend Mia came over. "Stir red and yellow," she said. "Watch this." Evan got his brush. He put red in the cup. He put yellow in the cup. He stirred it round and round. The paint turned orange! "Neat!" said Evan. He painted his pumpkin orange. It looked just like the one on the shelf.

Then Evan had an idea. He dipped his brush in blue. He stirred it with the yellow. The paint turned green! Mia laughed. "Now we can paint grass too," she said. Evan hurried to get more paper. "Green grass for my pumpkin," he said.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Many Muslims say 'Bismillah,' which means 'in the name of God,' before they eat.
story:
Ruby woke up from her nap at Grandma's house. Her tummy felt empty. "Time to eat," said Grandma. "We will have rice and warm bread."

Grandma put the big bowl on the table. Ruby grabbed her spoon fast. She opened her mouth wide.

"Wait, wait," said Grandma with a smile. "First we say Bismillah. It means in the name of God. Many Muslims say it before they eat."

Ruby put her spoon down. "Bismillah," she said. Grandma clapped. Then Ruby took a big bite of rice.

At dinner, Daddy drove over with a fuzzy blanket for Grandma. Ruby held her spoon and did not eat. "Say it with me," she told Daddy. Daddy laughed and said, "Bismillah." Then Ruby ate her bread all up.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: Feeling nervous on the first day of school is okay.
story:
Mason climbed the big school bus. He held his mama's hand. His tummy felt funny, like little wings flapping inside.

"Mama, my tummy is fluttery," he said.

Mama sat next to him by the window. The glass was cool when he touched it. "My tummy felt fluttery on my first day too," she said.

Mason looked up. "Even you?"

"Even me. It is okay to feel that way."

The bus went bump, bump, bump down the road. Mason watched out the window. A dog ran by a fence. The bus stopped, and a girl got on. She held a yellow backpack tight. Her face looked like Mason's tummy felt.

Mason patted the seat next to him. "You can sit here," he said. "My tummy is fluttery too."

The girl sat down. "My mama said that is okay," she said.

The bus stopped at the school. The driver smiled. "Here we are, friends," she said. Mason slid off the seat and waited while the doors folded open.

His tummy still fluttered a little. But now his mouth was smiling too. He took the girl's hand, and they walked up the steps together, into their classroom, where blocks sat in a happy red row by the window.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
story:
Amelia ran to the art room. Today she wore her new pink shirt. "No paint on it!" she said.

Her teacher held up a big red apron. "Put this on first," she said. "An apron keeps paint off your clothes." Amelia put her arms in. The apron went swish.

Then came the fun. "This is red," said Amelia. "This is yellow. This is blue." She knew all three. "Good work!" said her teacher.

Amelia wanted to mix. She dabbed red. She dabbed yellow. She stirred with her brush. The paint turned orange! "Ooh!" she said. She flicked her brush. A red dot flew. It landed on the apron, not her shirt. Amelia grinned and painted a big orange sun. "My favorite," she said.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: In English, we write from left to right across the page.
story:
Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He wanted to write his name all by himself. Miss Jo gave him a fat pencil and some paper.

Ryan held the pencil in his fist. Miss Jo showed him how to pinch it near the tip. "Like this," she said. Ryan tried it. The pencil felt better now.

He began his R at the right side of the page. He wrote R, then Y, then A. But then there was no room left. The N ran off the paper. Ryan frowned. His mouth turned sour.

He looked at the paper. He thought for a moment. Then he flipped it over and started at the left side. He wrote R, Y, A, N. This time every letter fit.

"I did it!" said Ryan.

Miss Jo clapped her hands. "Would you like a sticker?" she asked.

Ryan grinned and pointed at his name. "Can we write it again?"

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Feet leave footprints in fresh snow.
story:
Grayson woke up and saw white outside. "Snow!" he shouted. "No school today," said Mom. "It is a snow day."

Grayson wanted to play with his friend Sam. But first he wanted his red toy plane. It was lost! He had dropped it outside yesterday.

Mom put on his boots and coat. They stepped into the soft, fresh snow. Grayson looked down. His boots made marks in the snow. "Look, Mom! My feet make footprints!"

Then he saw more footprints. They were little ones. They went across the yard. "Maybe they know where my plane is," said Grayson. He followed the bumpy little footprints. Step, step, step. They went next door, to Sam's door!

Sam opened the door. He held the red plane. "You dropped it. I was bringing it back!" Grayson clapped his hands. "My footprints found you!" he said. "Come play in the snow," said Sam. And they did.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: A backpack is a bag you carry on your back.
story:
Felix was starting his first day of school. He wore his new backpack. It had a picture of a bear on it. "That is a backpack," said his mom. "It is a bag you carry on your back." Felix stood up straight in the playground.

But Felix could not run. His backpack was too heavy. He wanted to play on the wooden swing. He tried to walk fast. His back hurt a little. He sat down on a bench.

Then he opened his backpack. He looked inside. He had packed three toy cars and a big teddy bear. Felix took them out. He put them in his mom's bag. Now his backpack was light. Felix ran to the swing. He went up and down, up and down. A girl named Mia ran next to him. "Your backpack is small," she said. Felix laughed. "It is light now. And it still goes on my back."

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: A song can be played or sung fast or slow.
story:
Isabella went to Miss Jo's music room. She saw a shiny drum and a little stool with a cat on it. The cat had a long tail. "Hello, cat," said Isabella. She wanted to sing the whole rhyming song by herself.

First they tried it fast. "One, two, three, fast as can be!" The words got all tangled up. "Muddle-muddle-moo," said Isabella, and she laughed. The cat jumped off the stool.

"Let's try it slow," said Miss Jo. "One, two, slow and low." Isabella clapped her hands on her knees. Clap, clap, clap. The claps made a steady beat. The words came out just right, one by one. "I can do it slow!" said Isabella.

Then Miss Jo asked, "Fast or slow now?" Isabella grinned. "Slow first!" She sang it slow and clapped along. Then she tried it fast, and this time the words did not tangle. The cat came back and tapped its tail, one, two, one, two, right on the beat.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: Tablets are kept away from water and drinks.
story:
Zachary walked into the school computer lab. His teacher, Ms. Bell, smiled at him. "Today you will learn the tablet," she said. Zachary felt a little worried. "It looks big," he said. "I will stay right here," said Ms. Bell.

Zachary pressed the round button. The screen lit up! He pressed his finger on the drawing app. It opened. He drew a green pond with a fat blue frog. "Look!" he said. His friend Maya set her juice cup right beside the tablet. "Juice goes on the far table," said Ms. Bell. "Tablets are kept away from water and drinks." Maya carried her cup to the other table. Zachary was careful to keep his hands dry too.

Then it was time to go. Zachary pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the soft blue basket. "All done," he said. Ms. Bell clapped. "You did it all by yourself." Zachary ran to line up, still smiling at the dark screen in the basket.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: Families get a bed or sleeping spot ready for a guest who stays the night.
story:
Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Elizabeth ran to the guest bedroom. The bed was empty. There was no pillow on it. There was no blanket on it. Grandpa could not sleep like that.

Elizabeth went to the linen closet. She counted what she found. "One pillow, two pillows, three pillows," she said. She chose the softest one. It was big and white. She hugged it all the way to the guest room.

Next she looked for a blanket. She found her old blue blanket. It was warm and soft. She laid it on the bed. She tucked the edges in tight, like a little nest. "There," she said. "One bed, one pillow, one blanket, all ready for Grandpa."

That night Grandpa climbed into the bed. He patted the pillow. He pulled the blanket up to his chin. "This is the best bed," he said. "Did you make it ready for me?"

"Yes," said Elizabeth. "I got your sleeping spot all ready." Grandpa gave her a hug. She loved the smell of his sweater. "Good night, Grandpa," she said. "Sleep tight."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn.
story: Jasmine wanted to run to the swings. The sun was shiny and bright. "Stop," said Mom. "Let me put on your sunscreen." "Why?" asked Jasmine. Mom rubbed the cream on her nose and her neck and her arms. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn." Jasmine took Mom's hand and they walked to the swings. The wind blew. "It is windy today," said Jasmine. Her hair flew up like a flag. She held her hat with one hand. Big clouds came. Drip, drop. Rain fell on the slide. Mom opened an umbrella. "Rainy days need umbrellas," said Jasmine. They sat under it and watched the puddles grow. Then the rain stopped. Jasmine looked at her arms. No red spots. No sunburn at all. "The sunscreen worked," she said. Mom smiled. "Sunny, rainy, windy," said Jasmine. "Every day needs something different." She ran back to the swings and pumped her legs high, up into the shiny sun.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: When a grown-up reads a book aloud, they are reading the words, not just looking at the pictures.
story:
Mohamed wanted his turtle book at bedtime. He ran to get it. He held it out to Dad. "Read this one!"

Dad opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He read the words out loud. "Little turtle grew and grew." Mohamed looked at the black marks under the picture. "What are those little marks, Dad?"

"Those are words," said Dad. "I read the words. They tell the story." Dad's finger slid along the marks. The words came out of his mouth, one by one. Mohamed watched the finger. Then the words came again. He tapped the marks himself. Nothing came out of his mouth.

Then they came to a page with just a turtle. It was a big green turtle. There were no black marks on it at all. Mohamed pointed at it. "Read this page, Dad!"

Dad looked at the page. He turned his head this way and that. Then he shook his head. "There are no words here, Mohamed. There is nothing written on this page to read."

Mohamed leaned close. He looked and looked. The page felt smooth under his hand. No marks anywhere. Just the turtle, fast asleep in the sand. Mohamed sat very still and thought about that.

Dad turned to the last page. More little marks! Dad read them. "The dizzy turtle spun and spun, then slept." Mohamed giggled. He turned the book around in his hands. He looked at the marks upside down. They looked funny that way.

"Now you hold it," said Dad. "Turn the pages from the front, like this." Mohamed turned the pages, front to back, all by himself. He stopped at the big green turtle. He tapped the empty page. "No words here," he said. Dad smiled and kissed his head. Mohamed hugged the book tight to his chest.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a rainy day, a raincoat helps keep your body dry.
story:
The morning was sunny. Samuel put on his sun hat. He ran to the backyard to build a sand castle. Then the wind came. It was windy! His hat blew off. "Come back, hat!" he called. He put on his little jacket for the wind.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Samuel ran out to save his castle. The rain fell on his head and his shirt. He was all wet! He ran back to the door. "Mom, why am I wet?" he asked. "No raincoat," said Mom. "A raincoat helps keep your body dry." She helped him put it on. It was red with a happy hood.

Samuel went out again. The rain fell on the raincoat. He stayed dry! Dry, dry, dry. He touched his shirt under the coat. Not wet at all. Later the rain stopped. "Will we see snow today?" he asked. "No, just rain," said Mom with a smile. Samuel patted his quiet, dry castle and waved to the sky. "Bye bye, rain."

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, like the shape of a door.
story:
Naomi wanted to win the shape game. Mama had hidden shapes all over the playroom. "Find a circle," said Mama. Naomi found a round ball. It rolled when she pushed it. Soft and smooth.

"Now find a triangle," said Mama. Naomi held up a toy roof. It had three sides and pointy corners. "Triangle!" she said.

"Last one. Find a rectangle." Naomi looked and looked. She saw the play kitchen. She saw a toy fork on the little table. She was thirsty, so she took a sip from her cup.

Then she saw the door. She touched the side. One, two, three, four sides. She touched each corner. One, two, three, four square corners. "The door is a rectangle!" said Naomi. Mama clapped. Naomi laughed and patted the door.
